headline: Erethon / Papyrus
intro: The main technical work here is QuestsXL, a configurable scripting and content-authoring system for quests, events, world interactions, and instanced world state. Papyrus is the custom server foundation underneath it, including RPG systems and Paper fork work.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Developer, game designer, and project lead

hero.alt: Large Minecraft city landscape used in Erethon
hero.caption: A hub city in the persistent RPG world.

timeline.title: Designer-facing scripting
timeline.shortText: QuestsXL grew into a composable scripting system for quests and world events. Designers build content from actions, conditions, and objectives, with stages, callbacks, macros, runtime variables, math expressions, branching, and reusable snippets.

annotations.label: Objectives
annotations.detail: Objectives define player or event goals and can run callbacks when completed.

annotations.label: Actions
annotations.detail: Actions handle messages, rewards, spawning, dialogue, IBC changes, stage jumps, and more.

annotations.label: Conditions
annotations.detail: Conditions gate quest starts, actions, objectives, branches, and event activation.

timeline.outcome: Quest and event content can be authored, adjusted, and extended through YAML while core behavior stays centralized and maintainable.

timeline.title: Events as scripted world systems
timeline.shortText: QXL events use the same stage/action/objective model as quests, but are bound to the world instead of one player. They can auto-start from conditions, update while active, track participation, give tiered rewards, chain into other events, and act as building blocks for larger meta-events.

media.alt: Erethon event combat with bomb objective, enemy NPC, and objective tracker
media.caption: A scripted event encounter with combat objectives and world state.

annotations.label: Lifecycle
annotations.detail: Events move through states like waiting, active, completed, failed, and disabled.

annotations.label: Participation
annotations.detail: Combat progress and objective completion can feed participation and rewards.

annotations.label: Orchestration
annotations.detail: Actions can start other events or advance stages, making event chains and meta-events possible.

timeline.outcome: Designers can build repeatable world activity without each event needing custom plugin code.

timeline.title: World content tools
timeline.shortText: QXL also covers the surrounding world-content workflow: world interactions, daily and weekly quest rotations, regions, points of interest, instanced areas, and client-side block-state changes through Instanced Block Collections.

media.caption: QXL content can trigger dialogues, quests, events, world interactions, and staged world-state changes.

annotations.label: World interactions
annotations.detail: Location-based objective holders can start quests, react to blocks, or trigger one-time discoveries.

annotations.label: Instancing
annotations.detail: Regions and IBCs let content show per-player or per-group world states without changing the shared world for everyone.

annotations.label: Rotations
annotations.detail: Periodic quests support shared daily and weekly quest pools with completion rewards.

timeline.outcome: The tooling is not only for individual quests; it gives designers a broader content-authoring layer for the live world.

timeline.title: Reusable content patterns
timeline.shortText: The scripting layer supports macros, reusable reward snippets, runtime variables, score counters, optional objectives, manual stage progression, and command-triggered objectives. That makes it possible to build more complex content while keeping quest files readable.

media.caption: Reusable YAML patterns keep complex content maintainable.

annotations.label: Macros
annotations.detail: Common snippets can be defined once and called with parameters.

annotations.label: Runtime state
annotations.detail: Variables and score counters let content react to players, groups, and event state.

annotations.label: Branching
annotations.detail: Manual stage progression and impossible objectives support branching quest structures.

timeline.outcome: QXL is less a quest plugin and more a small content scripting platform for the server.

timeline.title: Papyrus and the Paper fork
timeline.shortText: Papyrus is built on Paper, but maintaining a server fork is its own engineering problem: working with Git patch workflows, reading deobfuscated Minecraft and Paper source, understanding undocumented internals, and keeping custom behavior compatible with upstream changes.

media.alt: Java code for a Spellbook skill
media.caption: Papyrus and Spellbook required working across custom plugin code, Paper internals, and Minecraft server behavior.

annotations.label: Patch workflow
annotations.detail: Paper forks are maintained through Git patches, not just normal plugin development.

annotations.label: Internals
annotations.detail: Changes often require reading deobfuscated Minecraft code and undocumented server behavior.

annotations.label: Compatibility
annotations.detail: Custom behavior has to survive upstream Paper and Minecraft changes.

timeline.outcome: This work built a better understanding of large unfamiliar codebases, Git patch maintenance, and server internals.

timeline.title: NPC load testing
timeline.shortText: Papyrus also had to handle large numbers of custom NPCs without eating the server tick budget. The test here shows roughly 300 attacking NPCs while the server stayed around 3ms per tick in the measured window.

media.alt: Minecraft performance test with roughly 300 attacking NPCs and server tick timing overlay
media.caption: NPC combat load test: around 300 attacking NPCs at roughly 3ms per tick.

annotations.label: Tick budget
annotations.detail: The server timing overlay shows the measured entity load stayed low enough for gameplay.

annotations.label: NPC count
annotations.detail: The scene contains hundreds of attacking NPCs, which is a useful stress case for combat AI.

timeline.outcome: This kind of test is important because RPG systems only matter if the server can still run them under real encounter load.

timeline.title: Combat and skill scheduling
timeline.shortText: Spellbook schedules skill activations across server ticks to keep combat responsive while distributing load across many entities.

media.alt: Graph representation of the Spellbook spell queue
media.caption: The Spellbook queue smooths skill execution under load.

annotations.label: Queue
annotations.detail: Skill activations are ordered instead of all competing inside the same tick.

annotations.label: Load
annotations.detail: Work can be distributed while preserving fair activation order.

timeline.outcome: Combat remains understandable and fair even when many players and NPCs use abilities.

timeline.title: Item stats and RPG data
timeline.shortText: Items, stats, rarity, levels, and generated modifiers are part of the configurable RPG layer. The goal is the same as with quests and events: keep the game rules data-driven so balance changes do not require rewriting core code.

media.alt: Minecraft item tooltip showing an RPG sword with level, rarity, and generated stats
media.caption: A basic generated item tooltip with RPG stats.

annotations.label: Item identity
annotations.detail: Level, equipment type, and rarity give designers useful balance axes.

annotations.label: Generated stats
annotations.detail: The item system can attach multiple stat modifiers without hardcoding each item.

timeline.outcome: The item layer gives the RPG economy and progression systems more room to be tuned through data.

timeline.title: Combat and economy design
timeline.shortText: Designed parts of the combat model, faction economy, progression structure, and PvP territory loop so the RPG systems had clear player-facing goals.

media.alt: Erethon minimap showing territory and world context
media.caption: World and territory context for faction gameplay.

annotations.label: Territory
annotations.detail: Faction control and conflict needed readable strategic goals.

annotations.label: Player routes
annotations.detail: The world layout had to support travel, conflict, and points of interest.

timeline.outcome: The design work connected custom systems to concrete reasons for players to build, fight, trade, and cooperate.

timeline.title: Configurable world rules
timeline.shortText: Mobs, faction buildings, economy outputs, events, and balance values are exposed through configuration so designers can iterate on the world without rebuilding the server.

media.caption: A building configuration that produces grain and affects nearby farmland.

annotations.label: Inputs
annotations.detail: Requirements encode balancing constraints around player-built structures.

annotations.label: Outputs
annotations.detail: Resource production and services can be tuned through data.

timeline.outcome: Designers can tune economy and world behavior through data while players still get the freedom of sandbox construction.

closing: The important part is the authoring model: much of Erethon is built as configurable systems first, so content can be changed by designers instead of requiring developer intervention for every quest, mob, event, interaction, or economy tweak.
